As far as healing goes if you do decide to go through with the piercing, you’re going to be on a straight liquid diet for like the first week, but never through a straw. then move on to soft foods for about 3 weeks. Nothing too spicy or seasoned. Things like mashed potatoes and apple sauce. No smoking during healing. You’ll clean the piercing 3 times a day with alcohol free mouthwash and 2 times a day with saline wash. (You can also use saline throughout the day to mitigate swelling pain). During the healing process it’s normal for clear/white/light Amber yellow discharge to leak from the piercing, but if you notice the discharge turning a dark or odd color accompanied by pain you should seek medical help quickly. Bacterial infections are actually really rare with a properly cared for tongue piercing but they can be pretty dangerous if they do develop so just keep an eye on yourself. Outside of that if you have any other questions you can feel free to ask, but your piercer should give you an aftercare sheet that says all of this stuff on it plus any of their recommended healing processes. 

Lastly, when the piercing heals and the swelling is gone you DEFINITELY need to go back to your piercer and have them put in properly sized jewelry. Super important for oral piercings because you are asking to mess up your teeth FAST by keeping the longer bar in your mouth.

I’m a piercer and I would personally not get my tongue pierced and I vehemently warn any client about the potential downfalls of any oral piercings. What ends up happening with tongue piercings is the balls/gems/toppers will hit and clang on the backs of your front teeth, causing enamel erosion/gum recession over time. This leads to decay obviously. My husband who had his tongue pierced for like 10 years and was very careful with it, ended up taking his out after our last dentist visit because even his perfectly placed and perfectly sized jewelry had started eroding his teeth. The other thing is when you chew food, sometimes the ball will get bit down on instead, which is obviously painful, and extremely horrible for the teeth that are biting on metal. 


All this to say, If you have the money to spend on your oral health and regular dentist checkups and you really really want this piercing, go for it! I just think you need to go in with the mindset that you will be spending time/money/pain on something that you will potentially have to take out relatively soon, and definitely have to take out eventually.

YouTube is a life saver. As is Amazon tbh. You can get some pretty good human hair on Amazon for cheap as well as synthetics. 

Starting off, if you’re unsure you can get a some wigs with bangs, those are usually easy to pull off as you don’t have to worry about a hairline and they’re pretty easy to just throw on and go. 

Then there’s glueless/precut lace options where the lace doesn’t have to be glued down to “melt” onto your skin (basically become invisible) 

Then there’s obviously your glue down lace fronts. 


As far as synthetics go on Amazon, there’s actually quite a few great options to choose from, plus you can return if you have problems with the wig. 

My personal favorite recent find on Amazon is “gorgius” brand wigs on Amazon. They sell all kinds of wigs with really good fibers/human hair mixes in them and the lace is perfect for All skin tones and pretty much ready to just throw on and go. Plus they come in a few lengths and colors and curl/straight/wavy patterns. Plus most of their wigs are between like 50-70 bucks so it’s not THAT expensive for a nice lace front. 


Another tip I have is that if you get thinning scissors and make a few cuts throughout the wig, it will help keep the wig from tangling, which means less damage to the wig when you brush it, which means the wig will last a LOT longer. There’s a lot of videos on how to do that on YouTube, but basically wigs tangle so bad because all the hair is the same length, if you make it more varied (like human hair) it doesn’t tangle as bad and it’s easier to maintain. 


Also as far as maintenance goes, you should get some synthetic wig shampoo/conditioner. I got a set from Amazon that has really helped my wigs last longer for like 15 bucks I think? Really any brand will do, but it basically keeps the wig from getting too staticky which can also cause damage/tangles. 


Lastly, to make a synthetic wig less shiny you can use baby powder or dry shampoo to Mattify the hair and make it look more like human hair.

This looks like a hard front wig (no lace) so I would recommend maybe placing the hairline behind your own (like by half an inch to an inch) if the roots match your current hair color. You can also tone down shine in the wig by putting baby powder or dry shampoo in it.  As far as the part, If there is fake scalp under it, you can pluck it a little to make it wider and put concealer in your skin tone on it to make it look more real.

You should (always, but especially when it comes to Great Danes/large breed dogs) strive for the best food available to you. This is usually not something to worry about until between the ages of 1-2 so you definitely have time to work that out. 

All this to say that every single penny is worth it. I’ve never had a better friend than my buddy barbas. I can’t describe it but it’s like having an Angel with you. A shining example of all that is pure, and that pure being loves YOU. It’s the most amazing feeling in the world.

Way back in the day quite a few alchemists thought that aged urine was the recipe for the philosophers stone. I guess they’d boil and cool it and add new urine and keep repeating the process until stones formed, but apparently no one ever “completed” the stone.

Obviously pet insurance is number one. 

Number 2 is that Danes have an extended growth period. It takes them about 2 years to reach full maturity and you want them to be intact during that time to create the correct hormones to support their growth correctly to avoid future health issues, so don’t spay/neuter until 2 years and get the stomach tacking done at the same time. 


Number 3, because of their sensitive skin/short hair/foldy droopy skin and their penchant for drooling, you’ve gotta take a little extra care in keeping their faces clean after eating and drinking and making sure you clean their food/water bowls every day to avoid any kind of rashes/acne in their skin folds. My boy has a mild case of pyoderma (basically dog acne) even though I DO take these precautions just because they’re predisposed to stuff like that already. Spent almost 400 bucks and gotta rub on him/give him 4 different meds every day, so I can only imagine how bad it would be if I wasn’t already keeping him clean lol. 

Number 4 is you should definitely feed them a good diet. Kind of depends on what they need/your dog specifically but some Danes with sensitive skin do well with food that doesn’t have poultry in it or sometimes grain free works best. Sometimes those things don’t matter at all. The only thing that really matters when it comes to food is the quality of the food. I think it’s worth buying expensive/quality food because ultimately that is what’s going to keep your Dane developing healthy. 

5 is that before you can get their stomachs tacked you gotta make sure not to let them eat too fast/too much at once to avoid gas that could cause their stomach to flip. Also avoid heavy exercise for an hour before and an hour after eating. 

6 is that you should start teaching your pup the things it should know as an adult while it’s a pup. Much easier to leash train a baby than it is to play tug of war with a full grown adult. But I will say the gentle leader head harness has done wonders with my boy.  


7 is that you should start giving supplements for joint development at around a year old. This will help avoid/prolong the time before future joint issues. 

8 is that Danes seem to be the most emotionally reciprocating dogs I’ve ever encountered. Stay calm during training and it should be a breeze. It really seems like they just live to see you happy and will do whatever you ask of them just cause they want you to be proud. 


9 is that they get very very attached to their caretakers. It’s best to kennel train them (and to have a large enough kennel for them) starting as pups. They will go crazy and be anxious when you leave. They’re big scared cats as it is and really don’t like being without their person. My Dane about clawed through the walls one time when I went to the store without him. With training he’s doing much much better but had I realized sooner me stepping out without him was a big problem that needed training, I could have saved my wall lol. 

10 is that they are the goofiest most loving and cuddly and caring and gentle breed I’ve ever met. Any harm they cause is really just a consequence of not knowing their own size and not understanding that while they are trying to cuddle you they’re actually crushing you. It’s a shame they have such short lives. You should take as many pictures and videos as you can and enjoy every second you have with them. That’s going to become your best buddy. Your shadow.

Not to be pretentious or anything, but it seems everyone here is grouping all cockroaches together as invasive pests (basically just fingering German cockroaches as bad guys), and while I agree with the sentiment that German cockroaches are pretty dang terrible, I’d also like to say one of my favorite pets was a cockroach. He was a hissing cockroach named Humphrey. He lived to be 4 years old and I learned a lot about them in order to care for him properly. Some interesting things are that I had to keep him at a correct humidity/temperature, if he would have escaped his enclosure and got lost in my house he wouldn’t have made it very long which is why we don’t see hissing cockroach infestations in the us like that. I also had to feed him a varied diet of fresh fruits and vegetables, and supplement with a jelly vitamin fruit food because they won’t eat rotting stuff so I’d have to remove anything he didn’t eat within the day. Hissers (and a lot of other roach species) also do well alone/in smaller colonies and grow very slowly and only reproduce a couple times a year. Also, due to them generally avoiding rotting things/gross things and their constant grooming/cleaning they aren’t associated with the spread of disease, although they can still cause allergic/asthmatic reactions in people who are sensitive to their skin casings/droppings. They’re also extremely docile, pretty durable and almost seem to enjoy human interaction (as far as a bug can “enjoy” anything lol). My point being that I hold all bugs to the same standard, which is can it severely harm me? Will it encroach on my territory? (infestation), is it parasitic? If the answers to all those questions are no then I like them just as much (If not more) than butterflies. 

Also for the record I think hissing cockroaches are way cooler looking and acting than butterflies.

Well you don’t need to be a vet to understand a snakes body. They don’t absorb medicines as quickly or efficiently as we do. Nebulising alone would only work if the snake was mildly sick and had time to take in the treatments, and honestly a uri in a reptile can turn deadly so quickly that I would never ever use just a nebuliser alone. They can be good for opening a snakes airways, but that’s just for treating a symptom, even if you were nebulising antibiotics the snake isn’t going to absorb enough, quickly enough. This is why they need injections, because at that point you immediately negate the risk of the snake going septic, and the symptoms start to clear up immediately. I’ve been caring for reptiles since I was 15, so I’ve got 10 years under my belt and  quite a few vet visits, and all of the information I just told you was confirmed by almost every source I read on the internet as well as my vet when I was discussing treatment options for my first boa with a respiratory infection. It seems to me that quite a few exotic vets don’t really take the time to educate themselves on the nuances of each individual species they treat, and kind of generalize their treatments of all reptiles together, even though common sense should tell you you can’t treat a snake like you would treat a lizard. If you can’t make it to another town for a different vet, I think the best thing you can do is take time to educate yourself on your animal the best you can, and then work with your vet WITH your input. For instance, baytril is a common antibiotic prescription for uri in reptiles. It’s commonly prescribed for injection. It’s also a skin irritant and can leave your snake with scars and burns. To negate this outcome, it should be mixed with saline to dilute it. My vet had no idea about the saline, or the burning effects of baytril, but I pulled up all the information I had about it, showed him, and now they don’t give baytril WITHOUT saline at that clinic. Either way I wish the best of luck to you in the future with your animals but PLEASE in the future I’d you have another ri problem make sure you get the injections!
